headline: Outgoing After Midnight: Bass Hugging Inlet Bottom While Blues Own the Surface
subhead: With the bay running warm, the real bass bite has moved to full dark on the last of the ebb — and the first scout reports for albies are starting to circle.
body_markdown:
I made a call this week that cost me a sunset session but paid off twice as hard at midnight. Instead of hitting the inlet at last light like the day boats, I waited for the outgoing to really get moving — an hour past the turn, current stacking hard against the jetty rocks — and fished straight through to 2 a.m. That's where the bass have been all month, and with this bay running warm the way it has, that's where they're staying.

Here's the read: surface temps out front have been sitting up in the mid-70s, which is above where a striper wants to work hard in daylight. So the fish that are here — and there are fish here — have pushed down into the deep hole on the east side of the inlet, the scour just inside the rock pile, and they're only really turning on to feed when the sun's been gone a few hours and the current's got some shoulder to it. I've been anchoring up on the last two hours of the outgoing, eeling live snake eels on a fish-finder rig with just enough weight to hold bottom in that 20-25 foot hole, and letting the current do the work. No retrieve, just patience. Landed a stretch of bass from 26 to a fat 34 inches over three nights this week, none of it fast, but steady enough that I kept rebaiting. Bunker chunks on a 5/0 circle hook worked the same water when the eels ran short — bluefish showed up on those too, which tells you the blues are pushing right into the same current seam as the stripers after dark, not just chopping bait on top like they do at noon.
8
The daytime picture out front is a different animal entirely, and this is where the warm water is doing exactly what it's supposed to — favoring the bluefish over the bass. If you want a bent rod in daylight, work the beach off Tiana on peanut bunker schools with a stainless popper or a Ava jig on wire, retrieved fast through the surface commotion. That fishery has been consistent, not spectacular, but reliable enough to fill an afternoon while you wait for dark. Just don't expect quality stripers mixed in there right now — they've gone nocturnal and they're not coming back to the surface in 78-degree water to prove a point.

Ponquogue Bridge has been my other stop, and the weakfish have cooperated better than I expected given how warm the bay's gotten. Incoming tide, an hour before and after the top, working the shadow lines under the span with a 1/4-ounce bucktail dressed in white bucktail hair, tipped with a strip of squid or a sandworm. The weakfish sit right on the current edge where the bridge lights meet the dark water, and they'll hit that jig on the drop more than the retrieve. Fish have run 16 to 20 inches, a few keepers mixed with a lot of shorts, which is about the honest state of that fishery this summer — worth the trip, not a guarantee.

Fluke in the bay have been the most dependable thing going, if you're willing to move around and find the right piece of bottom. The channel edges off Tiana and the drop-offs on the west side of the canal mouth have both been holding fish — drift with a white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a 3/4-ounce bucktail, tipped with a strip of fluke belly for scent, and cover ground slow on the last two hours of the outgoing when the bait gets pulled off the flats into the channel. Keepers mixed with plenty of shorts, nothing blitz-level, but a few solid fish in the 20-22 inch range came out of that program this week. The canal itself has had some traffic too — a handful of guys working the current there into the Peconic side have picked up stray weakfish and fluke moving through on the tide swap, which tells me there's still exchange happening between the two systems even with the water warm on both ends.

We flagged this zone last week as one to watch for the season's first albie or bonito scout, and there's been some bait movement worth noting — small sand eels and rain bait pushing through the inlet rips on the last of the ebb, exactly the kind of forage that pulls false albacore in tight to structure once the temperature threshold gets crossed. Nothing confirmed yet, no hookups, but the ingredients are lining up faster than they usually do this early in August, and this stretch of beach has a habit of showing signs before Montauk does.

Looking ahead, the tide cycle is easing down toward neap over the next few days before it starts rebuilding toward the August 12 new moon, and I expect that softer current to push the bass even deeper and more strictly nocturnal for a stretch — less water movement means less reason for them to commit outside of full dark. If the warm, stable pattern holds like it has, I'd keep working the inlet hole late and let the bridge and bay structure fill in the daylight hours. If a cold front or a squall line comes through and knocks the surface temp down even two degrees, watch for the bass to show a little more willingness at dusk instead of waiting for 1 a.m. — that's the kind of shift that changes my whole schedule for a week. Until then, I'll be out there after most of the town's gone to bed, eel bucket in the boat, waiting on the tide.
